patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm: free the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: free the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes Linux kernel memory management by freeing the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio when it's loaded from zswap, which reduces the cost of exit time and improves system performance. The patch addresses an issue where dirty folios left in the swap cache caused significant delays during exit, particularly on large production workloads. By releasing the swap cache at swapin, the patch eliminates this overhead and results in a 15% decrease in exit time on a production workload.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) suggested a more readable and simplified version of the condition, but questioned whether this code should be zswap-specific, implying that it may not belong in common code.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a dirty swapin folio is reclaimed, which can lead to a memory leak.

Reviewer noted that do_swap_page() can find a dirty folio in the swap cache due to various reasons, not just zswap, and requested consideration of these cases.
sentiment_signals: zswap is simply the common case
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi David,

On Thu, Nov 26, 2026 at 1:54 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

I am mostly interested in the zswap benefits, but nothing is zswap
specific here: do_swap_page() can also find a dirty folio in the swap
cache when reclaim bailed out before writeout, or when the swap write
failed. In all those cases, the copy in the slot is stale, so the slot
only reserves swap space. zswap is simply the common case, since
zswap_load() dirties the folio.

What do you think?

Thanks,

Alex

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David questioned the generality of the patch description and suggested that it should focus solely on zswap, also recommending additional measurements without zswap. He pointed out a potential issue with the 'folio is dirty' condition being linked to exclusive access, and proposed an alternative condition for freeing the swap cache.
review_comments.raw_body:
If it's generic, then the comment shouldn't mention zswap in the comment :)

And the patch description should be all about zswap.

And we should measure the effect without zswap.

So, folio dirty -> We'd need another writeback because the content on disk is stale.

If we reclaim swap, the next reclaim run will have to re-allocate one.


But why is this "is dirty" linked to exclusive?

What if we did

/*
 * Free the swapcache if the folio is already dirty, or if we will dirty it
 * immediately afterwards by writing to it.
 */
if (folio_test_dirty(folio))
	return true;
return (fault_flags & FAULT_FLAG_WRITE) && exclusive;

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio is being swapped in and its swap slot is already reserved, which can lead to a deadlock when trying to free the swap cache

The reviewer suggested that the patch description should mention zswap as an example of a scenario where the problem occurs, rather than implying it's the sole motivation. They also noted that caching swap slots can lead to unnecessary pageout work in subsequent reclaim attempts and requested genericization of this logic.

Reviewer Nhat Pham suggested removing the 'exclusive' check in do_swap_page(), citing that folio_free_swap() already handles necessary safety checks.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 26, 2026 at 9:20 AM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

+1. Maybe mention zswap as an example of when this can happen rather
than the sole motivation. I suspect this is a generic problem, with
zswap being a common/easy to trigger case :)

In general, seems like the whole point of caching these slots
(especially after Kairui optimized the swap allocator) is just to
avoid repeating pageout work in subsequent reclaim attempts. In zswap
case (where we invalidate the fault after page-in), that trade-off is
not worth it.

FWIW, zram is also doing the same thing:

/*
 * Always try to free swap cache for SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO devices. Swap
 * cache can help save some IO or memory overhead, but these devices
 * are fast, and meanwhile, swap cache pinning the slot deferring the
 * release of metadata or fragmentation is a more critical issue.
 */
if (data_race(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO))
    return true;

so we kinda already have some backend-specific logic bled out to this
location. Maybe we can genericize this in the future :)

---

I don't think we need exclusive here at all yeah. folio_free_swap()
already does all the necessary safety checks.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: scrub: size read bios to the bwlimit 10ms burst

version_history.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: scrub: size read bios to the bwlimit 10ms burst

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the size of read bios in Btrfs scrub to be more burst-aware, taking into account the specified bandwidth limit and its duration. The goal is to avoid submitting large bios that would lead to long sleeps, which can cause pacing issues at lower bandwidth limits. Instead, the code computes a burst size based on the bandwidth limit and duration, and uses this value to determine the bio size. This approach allows for more natural pacing of I/O operations, especially at higher bandwidth limits. The patch also introduces a throttle variable to skip throttling parity reads during scrubs.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 3/4] btrfs: scrub: handle bwlimit below 512KiB
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch updates the Btrfs scrub's throttling mechanism to handle bandwidth limits below 512KiB/s. The existing implementation had a practical minimum limit of 512KiB/s due to its interval-based approach, but this update introduces a burst duration concept that allows for more flexible and efficient throttling at lower limits. At higher limits, the patch still uses the original interval-based approach to avoid excessive sleeping overhead. Additionally, it adds a wake-up/cancel path when changing the limit to improve responsiveness.

> do_add_efi_memmap() has no case for EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY and adds the
> same range again as E820_TYPE_RESERVED. e820__update_table() resolves
> the overlap in favour of the reserved type, so the kernel never uses
> the range.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Do not signal event 0 to a masked PE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents event 0 from being signaled to a masked Performance Extension (PE) in the ARM SDEI firmware driver. When a PE is masked, it should not receive event 0 signals, which can cause other CPUs to hang. The patch introduces a lock and flag system to ensure that event 0 is only signaled to unmasked PEs. It also updates the cpu_pm notifier to correctly handle masking and unmasking of PEs. This fix addresses issues with CPU hangs and panics caused by event 0 signals being sent to masked PEs.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the implementation of sdei_event_signal() and how it handles event 0 signals to masked PEs. They explain that senders signal a PE only under its lock, and if the PE is masked, they wait for any pending signals to arrive before masking. The author also provides code changes to implement this behavior.

review_comments.author: YinFengwei
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer YinFengwei pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where a PE is masked due to SDEI_PE_MASKED, and suggested adding a check for this condition in sdei_event_signal()

The reviewer questioned whether the lock should be taken in a specific scenario where the panic did not acquire the lock, suggesting that it should be handled similarly to the 'else' path.

Reviewer YinFengwei questioned the use of a specific read operation in the patch and suggested replacing it with READ_ONCE() to ensure memory ordering
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Kirill,

On Tue, Nov 24, 2026 at 07:47:04PM +0000, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) wrote:

---

If the panic didn't take the lock, should lock be taken
just like "else" path?

---

I am wondering whether READ_ONCE() should be used here?


Regards
Yin, Fengwei

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed YinFengwei's concern that sdei_event_signal() could hang if another CPU holds the lock when it tries to signal a masked PE, explaining that in this scenario the other CPU was stopped and would never drop the lock. The author concluded that there is no need for a trylock because the sender has either counted its signal or never sent one.

Author responded to feedback about the potential for a race condition between loading and storing the unmasked flag, explaining that the notifier runs with IRQs off and only this CPU writes the flag, making it safe.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a lockup issue on idle CPUs caused by SDEI NMI backtraces. The problem occurs when an event is signaled to all CPUs, including those in a power-down state where SDEI is masked. To fix this, the patches prevent event 0 from being sent to masked PEs and send regular backtrace IPIs to these CPUs instead. This approach ensures that the system remains responsive even during idle states.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern that the patch does not address the issue of TF-A refusing to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks right after the check still takes the SGI. The author explains that this is due to the handshake change since the earlier version and asks Jinjie to run the new version on HIP12.
review_comments.raw_body:
The SDEI NMI backtrace signals event 0 to every other CPU, including the
ones in a power-down idle state, where the kernel has SDEI masked. TF-A
acknowledges the SGI behind event 0 on a masked PE and never ends it,
and the PE takes no Non-secure interrupt again. Jinjie hit it on a
384-CPU HIP12, where one sysrq-l locked up the machine.

Patch 1 keeps event 0 away from masked PEs. Patch 2 sends the regular
backtrace IPI to the CPUs that SDEI refused, which wakes them.

TF-A v2.13 and later refuse to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks
right after the check still takes the SGI. The TF-A fix is under review:

  https://review.trustedfirmware.org/c/TF-A/trusted-firmware-a/+/55414

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, which takes into account the migratetype of the request when checking if an allocation can succeed. The function is used in several places where the caller needs to know whether the allocation will honor ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests. The patch also moves the declaration of __zone_watermark_ok() to mm/page_alloc.h and makes no functional changes yet, as it's a preparation for future changes that will make the high-order check respect ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag. When this flag is set, the check should not consider free pages from other migration types when allocating a high-order request. This change aims to prevent fragmentation and improve performance under memory pressure conditions. The patch also updates the compaction logic to take into account the new watermark check and ensures that allocations do not stall in compaction unnecessarily. As a result, the patch is expected to reduce the number of stalls and failures during 64K mTHP faults under swap pressure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/9] mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the __get_user_pages() function by walking multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call, reducing the number of restarts and lock acquisitions. The patch achieves this by computing the walk end from the inclusive end address, rather than using pmd_addr_end(), which can lead to unsigned-long overflow on 2-level page tables. Additionally, it defers resolving none PTEs in hugetlbfs VMAs until after unlocking. A failure on the first PTE is returned to the caller, while subsequent failures are treated as short reads and retried by __get_user_pages(). The patch modifies the follow_page_pte() function to walk multiple PTEs and commit every page found.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the performance of slow GUP (get user pages) by batching whole PTE tables and reducing the number of page table descents. The current implementation resolves and commits one PTE per call, leading to a restart of the pgd/p4d/pud/pmd descent for every page. This series refactors the code in reviewable steps, introducing helpers and splitting out functions to improve performance. The patches include breaking out gup_fill_pages() and gup_flush_pages() helpers, converting follow_page_mask() to return a long, and walking multiple PTEs per call. The result is a significant reduction in get time for large folios, with median times reduced by up to 12.8x.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledges a potential issue where FOLL_WRITE GUP can miss COW faults due to exclusive PTEs in a mTHP folio, and agrees to add checks similar to those for FOLL_PIN.
review_comments.raw_body:
The sequence seems somewhat contrived, but it
looks like it can happen, and some runtimes
(maybe Java?) might actually do stuff like this.

1) mmap 64K private anon, touch it (one mTHP folio, 16 pages).

2) fork, child exits/execs

3) Parent holds 16 pages, all PTEs read-only

4) Parent writes first page, COW makes it exclusive. 
   This is now the only PageAnonExclusive page in the mTHP,
   while the other pages in the folio are not.

5) mprotect the range read-only. Now all PTEs are read-only,
   but the head is exclusive, while the 15 tails not.

6) Slow GUP pin_user_pages(FOLL_FORCE|FOLL_WRITE), which
   pins all 16 pages without COW faults, since all the
   PTEs have the same permissions, they all map the
   same folio, and the first page is PageAnonExclusive.

7) mprotect the range read-write again, this changes the
   first PTE (on an exclusive page) back to read-write,
   but GUP already did its thing

8) A write by the program to page 5 now causes a
   COW fault, since that page is not PageAnonExclusive,
   and the refcount is raised
 
9) A write to page 5 by the GUP buffer holder
   goes to the old page, and becomes invisible
   to the program

The fix is to simply do the same checks for
FOLL_WRITE that we already have in place for
FOLL_PIN.

Want me to put the above explanation in the
changelog, or tweak it some more?

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the aggregation (agg) page pool recycle ring size calculation for the Broadcom NIC driver (bnxt). The issue was caused by an incorrect divisor used to calculate the fill level of the agg queues, leading to an under-sized recycle ring. The fix divides the fill level by the number of buffers per allocation, using the maximum of the page size and rx_page_size as the divisor. This change ensures that the recycle ring is properly sized for different kernel configurations and buffer sizes, preventing memory leaks in certain scenarios.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] eth: bnxt: fix the agg page pool ring size on 64K-page kernels

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue in the Broadcom bnxt driver where the aggregate (agg) page pool ring size is incorrectly calculated on 64K-page kernels. The problem arises because the divisor used to calculate the ring size is always 1 when rx_page_size is 32K, leading to a cache that can hold twice as many pages as the agg ring uses. This causes memory waste and can lead to issues like reduced cached memory. To fix this, the patch changes the divisor to be the larger of PAGE_SIZE and rx_page_size, restoring the original size calculation.

review_comments.raw_body:
Ummm, yes, you are right :) With rx_page_size as the denominator,
agg_size_fac is the number of buffers per page pool allocation, which
is what f7dbedba6312 intended. I think the proper fix is below:

---

From: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
Date: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:24:04 -0800
Subject: [PATCH] eth: bnxt: fix the agg page pool recycle ring size
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit

Commit f7dbedba6312 ("eth: bnxt: take page size into account for page
pool recycling rings") sized the recycle ring of the agg page pool in
pages, dividing the agg ring size by the number of agg buffers per page.
Commit c55bf90a2112 ("eth: bnxt: adjust the fill level of agg queues
with larger buffers") changed the divisor to rx_page_size /
BNXT_RX_PAGE_SIZE, which is wrong in two cases:

- On 64K-page kernels rx_page_size can only be 32K, so the divisor is
  1, although each 64K page holds two agg buffers. With 1024 RX
  descriptors the agg ring posts 2048 buffers in 1024 pages, while the
  recycle ring can cache 2048 pages, or 128 MiB per RX queue.

- When a memory provider sets rx_page_size above PAGE_SIZE, each buffer
  is its own allocation and the fill level is already divided by
  rx_page_size / BNXT_RX_PAGE_SIZE. Dividing again gives a 4K kernel
  with 16K buffers a 256-entry ring for 1024 posted buffers.

Divide the fill level by the number of buffers per allocation,
max(PAGE_SIZE, rx_page_size) / rx_page_size. Nothing changes for
kernels with pages of 32K or less that use the default buffer size.

On a 64K arm64 host with a BCM57508 (32 queues, 1024 RX descriptors), a
TCP receiver that drained its sockets every 1.5 s left about 1.8 GiB
less memory in the agg page pools after the fix, 64 MiB per busy queue.

Fixes: c55bf90a2112 ("eth: bnxt: adjust the fill level of agg queues with larger buffers")
Suggested-by: Bjrn Tpel <bjorn@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
---
 drivers/net/ethernet/broadcom/bnxt/bnxt.c | 3 ++-
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/drivers/net/ethernet/broadcom/bnxt/bnxt.c b/drivers/net/ethernet/broadcom/bnxt/bnxt.c
index 52606db3f7b4a8..85ce4b2e297ecb 100644
--- a/drivers/net/ethernet/broadcom/bnxt/bnxt.c
+++ b/drivers/net/ethernet/broadcom/bnxt/bnxt.c
@@ -3948,7 +3948,8 @@ static int bnxt_alloc_rx_page_pool(struct bnxt *bp,
 				   struct bnxt_rx_ring_info *rxr,
 				   int numa_node)
 {
-	unsigned int agg_size_fac = rxr->rx_page_size / BNXT_RX_PAGE_SIZE;
+	unsigned int agg_size_fac = max(PAGE_SIZE, rxr->rx_page_size) /
+				    rxr->rx_page_size;
 	const unsigned int rx_size_fac = PAGE_SIZE / SZ_4K;
 	struct page_pool_params pp = { 0 };
 	struct page_pool *pool;
-- 
2.53.1-Meta

---

Letting rx-buf-len go below 32K on 64K kernels would be one way to do
it maybe? Although I guess that is something for net-next and not a fix.

Thanks for the review!
Usama

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reduces the size of the stage-2 page cache in KVM for arm64 hosts with 64 KiB pages, from 40 to 8 entries. This change is motivated by the observation that most of the cached pages are never used and the actual memory requirements are much lower than previously assumed. The new value still covers the minimum required for a stage-2 fault and leaves room for additional table allocations. The patch affects only arm64 hosts with 64 KiB pages, leaving other configurations unchanged.

Subject: [PATCH] KVM: arm64: Shrink the stage-2 memcache to the page-table
 depth

When a stage-2 fault may need new page tables, KVM first tops up the
vCPU's memcache: if it holds fewer pages than the fault might need, it
is refilled to KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE, which arm64 sets to
40. Pages never return to the cache, and unused ones stay there until
the vCPU is destroyed.

The cache only has to cover a single map: every fault that can allocate
tables tops it up first, and a map allocates at most one table per
level below the preallocated root (kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages()). That is
at most three pages with 4 KiB and 16 KiB pages, and two with 64 KiB
pages.

last-level table covers 512 MiB, an 8 GiB guest needs just 17 table
pages to map all of its memory, while its four vCPU caches get filled
with 160. On a production host with 64 KiB pages running 101 VMs with
four vCPUs each, the caches were still 86% full. The memory used:

                        before      after
  per-vCPU capacity     2.5 MiB     256 KiB
  all 404 vCPUs         869 MiB     <= 101 MiB

which is 4 pages and covers the deepest walk with one page to spare. On
the host above, it frees at least 768 MiB. Refills get more frequent,
but no more than four pages per vCPU ever sit unused. With 4 KiB pages,
the cache shrinks from 160 KiB to 16 KiB per vCPU.

Move the two level definitions to asm/kvm_types.h, so that the generic
top-up code in kvm_main.c can see them. kvm_pgtable.h still gets them
through linux/kvm_types.h.

The temporary cache in kvm_phys_addr_ioremap() uses the same capacity,
but it is topped up before every page it maps. The pKVM hypervisor
memcache and the eager split cache don't use this capacity.

niche configuration that hardly anyone uses. But the scale of the
numbers strike me a bit: 808GB worth of guest memory, and you're
complaining about 869MB? That's roughly 0.1% of the total, and the
savings you're gaining are even less... I know memory is expensive,
but you'd save a lot more than that by using a realistic page size.
Just saying...

I also question the assumption you are making that the guest is
strictly using IPA contiguous memory, and that therefore a very small
set of pages are all you need to map a guest. Guests with multiple,
disjoint memslots are (sadly) extremely common, specially in these
days of tiered memory and other random horrors.

account. And then you adjust it by whatever fudge factor seems

    -> kvm_pgtable_stage2_map()

        -> stage2_map_walker_try_leaf()
	  -> stage2_leaf_mapping_allowed()
	    -> kvm_block_mapping_supported() [ if false, allocate a page table ]

static bool kvm_block_mapping_supported(const struct kvm_pgtable_visit_ctx *ctx, u64 phys)
{
	u64 granule = kvm_granule_size(ctx->level);

	...

	if (granule > (ctx->end - ctx->addr))
		return false;

	...
}

But page table size can vary in NV between host and guest (guest must be >=
host) and it gets clamped to the smaller of the two in kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size():

static short kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
				     struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi,
				     struct vm_area_struct *vma)
{
	...
	if (s2fd->nested) {
		...
		/*
		 * If we're about to create a shadow stage 2 entry, then we
		 * can only create a block mapping if the guest stage 2 page
		 * table uses at least as big a mapping.
		 */
		max_map_size = min(kvm_s2_trans_size(s2fd->nested), max_map_size);
		...
	}
}

This sets s2vi->vma_pagesize based on this value:

static int kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
				     struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi)
{
	...
	s2vi->vma_pagesize = BIT(kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size(s2fd, s2vi, vma));
	...

And the fault map uses this in the mapping size, which defines ctx->addr, end
above in kvm_block_mapping_supported():

static int kvm_s2_fault_map(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
			    const struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi,
			    enum kvm_pgtable_prot prot,
			    void *memcache,
			    struct kvm_s2_fault_result *result)

	...
	mapping_size = s2vi->vma_pagesize;
	...
			ret = KVM_PGT_FN(kvm_pgtable_stage2_map)(pgt, gfn_to_gpa(gfn), mapping_size,
							 __pfn_to_phys(pfn), prot,
							 memcache, flags);
	...
}

So basically, if the host has smaller page table size than the guest, you need
an extra page table level.

So simple solution is to add nested to the check:

        if (!perm_fault || memslot_is_logging(s2fd->memslot) ||
            is_protected_kvm_enabled() || s2fd->nested) {
                ret = topup_mmu_memcache(s2fd->mmu, memcache);
                if (ret)

        }

But honestly I wonder at this point if it's truly worth doing all these checks?
Maybe safer to just topup unconditionally.

It'll only top up once before the cache is full anyway, so it's low cost. And
would make more consistent with other fault paths too.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] eth: bnxt: fix the agg page pool ring size on 64K-page kernels
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Broadcom NIC driver (bnxt) that affects the size of the aggregate page pool recycle ring on 64K-page kernels. The issue arises from incorrect calculation of the fill level, which is divided by the number of buffers per allocation instead of just the buffer size. This leads to under-sized rings and reduced memory efficiency. The patch corrects this by dividing the fill level by the maximum of the page size and the rx_page_size, ensuring that the ring size is correctly calculated for both 64K-page kernels and systems with larger buffer sizes.
